https://thecolu.mn/4187/romanian-city-ba.text: Politics July 24, 2026 Romanian City Bans Pride Parade Oradea, a western Romanian city, refuses for the fourth consecutive time to grant a permit for a Pride march. As Ark Oradea reported, city authorities again rejected the plan for the demonstration scheduled for this Saturday. With about 180,000 residents, Oradea remains the only major European city where the municipal government repeatedly blocks Pride events. Facebook | According to Ark Oradea’s chair, Iulian Dițiu, organizers submitted more than 100 potential route options beforehand. The city administration rejected them on Wednesday, citing alleged overlaps with other events and construction work. In previous years, the administration had also dismissed the plans for technical or administrative reasons. A statement from the mayor, who belongs to a Christian-conservative party, is not available. The organizers announced they would proceed with the demonstration on Saturday despite the lack of permission—under the motto “Oradea is for everyone.” Dițiu described the situation as both encouraging and disappointing. Last year participants had to pay fines Last year, between 500 and 600 people gathered for an unsanctioned march, resulting in fines for about nine participants totaling roughly €4,000. For this year’s demonstration, representatives from several diplomatic missions as well as the Romanian Ombudsperson for Human Rights have confirmed their attendance. The case has drawn international criticism: more than 150 organizations from 30 countries urged Romanian authorities to uphold the EU-wide right to freedom of assembly. They warned that the systematic ban on Pride marches signals a rollback of democratic standards and the rule of law. The European Union also chastises the Romanian authorities. Equality Commissioner Hadja Lahbib of Belgium and Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath of Ireland weighed in. In a social-media message, they stated: “People in Oradea should be able to demonstrate peacefully for their rights, just as in any other European city, and come together without fear.” Facebook | A week earlier, the United Nations rights commissioner, Michael O’Flaherty, warned: “I am concerned about reports that the CSD Oradea 2026 is being blocked again in Romania. The right to freedom of assembly applies to everyone. Authorities should coordinate with organizers to provide a safe and appropriate route and protect participants.” There have been earlier attempts in Poland and, more recently, in Hungary, to ban demonstrations for queer rights. The European Court of Human Rights had already ruled against Poland in 2007 for a CSD prohibition (TheColu.mn reported). This violated, among other things, the guaranteed freedom of assembly and the prohibition of discrimination under the European Convention on Human Rights. (dk) Marcy Ellerton My name is Marcy Ellerton, and I’ve been telling stories since I could hold a pen. As a queer journalist based in Minneapolis, I cover everything from grassroots activism to the everyday moments that make our community shine. When I’m not chasing a story, you’ll probably find me in a coffee shop, scribbling notes in a well-worn notebook and eavesdropping just enough to catch the next lead. International archaeology forum opens in Poznań Researchers from around the world are gathering in Poznań this week for the 21st World Congress of the International Union of Prehistoric and Protohistoric Sciences, known as UISPP 2026. The five-day meeting runs from 31 August to 4 September at Adam Mickiewicz University, where the university’s Faculty of Archaeology is helping to organise the programme. The congress is being held in Poland for the first time. Adam Mickiewicz University expects approximately 800 participants, making the event one of the largest international academic meetings hosted by the university this year. Its theme, “Archaeology in Motion: Past Lessons, Future Responsibilities”, places research methods, interpretation and the long-term responsibilities of archaeology at the centre of the discussion. The opening ceremony is scheduled for 31 August in the university’s Aula. The programme includes a keynote lecture by Barbara Barich of Sapienza University of Rome, alongside welcome addresses from the university and UISPP. Further sessions during the week will bring together specialists working on different periods, regions and archaeological approaches. From field evidence to broader questions UISPP describes its world congress as a platform for prehistoric and protohistoric research across geographical and disciplinary boundaries. The Poznań edition includes academic sessions, plenary lectures and meetings of specialist commissions. The format allows researchers to compare evidence from distant regions while also examining how new tools and changing public expectations are influencing archaeological work. That breadth is reflected in the congress motto. “Archaeology in Motion” points not only to the movement of past communities, objects and ideas, but also to the changing practice of archaeology itself. Researchers increasingly combine excavation with laboratory analysis, digital documentation, environmental studies, landscape research and public history. The meeting offers an opportunity to discuss how those strands can be connected without losing sight of the evidence on which interpretations depend. The organisers have also built a substantial programme around Poland’s archaeological heritage. Scientific excursions are planned to sites and institutions including Ostrów Lednicki, Gniezno, Biskupin, Krzemionki, Raj Cave, Kraków and the Wieliczka Salt Mine. Delegates will also visit the Archaeological Museum in Poznań, linking the academic programme with collections and places that document different stages of the region’s past. Poznań’s role as a research meeting place Hosting the congress strengthens Poznań’s profile as a centre for archaeological education and research. Adam Mickiewicz University is one of Poland’s major research universities, and its Faculty of Archaeology provides the institutional base for the event. For students and early-career researchers, an international congress of this scale can offer access to specialist discussions, professional networks and examples of research practice from outside Poland. The event also connects university work with the city’s cultural infrastructure. Poznań’s historic centre, museums and nearby archaeological sites form part of the setting in which the congress is taking place. This relationship matters for a field that depends on both specialist knowledge and public engagement. Archaeological research gains value when discoveries are documented carefully, interpreted responsibly and made understandable to communities. International academic gatherings can also have a practical effect beyond the conference rooms. They create opportunities to compare standards, develop joint research ideas and exchange experience in conservation, fieldwork and heritage presentation. The excursions planned for UISPP 2026 give visiting researchers a direct view of how Polish institutions preserve and communicate archaeological evidence. Looking towards future responsibilities The congress comes at a time when archaeology is addressing several connected questions: how to use increasingly sophisticated analytical technologies, how to protect sites and landscapes, and how to make research accessible while maintaining scholarly accuracy. These issues are relevant not only to specialists but also to schools, museums, local authorities and communities whose identities are connected to historic places. By bringing those questions into one international programme, UISPP 2026 presents archaeology as an active research discipline rather than a study limited to the distant past. The meeting’s focus on future responsibilities highlights the need to balance discovery with documentation, preservation and open communication. For Poznań, the congress provides a week-long concentration of expertise. For Poland, it marks the country’s first opportunity to host the UISPP World Congress. Its combination of international research, university teaching and visits to archaeological heritage sites makes the event a constructive development in the country’s science and education calendar.
